messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

The morning of the accident, Clara had been booked for a charity fashion show at a downtown hotel. She was sixty-six, still striking on a runway, and the job felt like a small victory against time. The show was chaotic—volunteer stagehands, a too-tight backstage corridor, and a young photographer named Marcus who kept backing into people while adjusting his lens. During the finale walk, Clara saw Marcus step backward onto the riser where a heavy lighting stand was balanced. She was ten feet away, her heel catching on a cable. She saw the stand tip. She saw his head turn a fraction too late. The crash of metal and glass was followed by a silence that seemed to last forever, and then Marcus was on the ground, blood pooling under his ear, his leg bent at an angle that should not be possible. Clara had not screamed. She had not even moved. She had stood there, frozen, while other people rushed forward. The paramedics said later that Marcus would recover, but he would walk with a limp for the rest of his life. Clara had come to believe that if she had been faster, if she had shouted, if she had simply moved her body instead of standing like a mannequin, the whole thing would not have happened. Somebody else would have known what to do. Somebody else would not have gotten into that situation in the first place.

In the months that followed, Clara found that her body had become a stranger to her. She could not relax, even when she was alone in her apartment with the door locked and the curtains drawn. Her muscles stayed tight, her shoulders hunched, her jaw clenched, as if she were bracing for a blow that never came. This constant physical vigilance bled into everything. She had difficulty concentrating on simple tasks—reading a magazine, following a television show, remembering whether she had taken her blood pressure medication. The tension in her body became a kind of background hum that drowned out everything else, and the longer it lasted, the more she felt that the accident had permanently broken something inside her. She told herself that a normal person would have moved on by now, would have stopped reliving the image of Marcus on the floor. But Clara could not stop, and her inability to let go became, in her own mind, further proof that she was fundamentally flawed. She felt permanently humiliated by what had happened, as if the whole world had seen her stand there, useless, and had marked her as someone who freezes when it matters. She would never forgive herself for not doing more to stop it.

The avoidance was subtle at first. She declined a booking for another charity show, then another. She stopped going to the grocery store during busy hours because the crowds made her feel trapped and watchful. She told her daughter she was just tired. But the real reason was that every time she left her apartment, her body went on high alert. She scanned sidewalks for trip hazards, for people moving unpredictably, for anything that might require her to react. The hypervigilance was exhausting, and the exhaustion fed her conviction that she was not safe anywhere, that she could not trust herself to keep anyone—including herself—out of harm's way. Her agent called less often. Clara let the calls go to voicemail. She had come to believe that she did not deserve to stand on a runway anymore, that her face and her body had become symbols of her failure. The career that had sustained her for forty years was quietly slipping away, and she did not have the energy to stop it.

What finally brought Clara to therapy was a panic attack in her own living room. She had been watching a television show in which a character stumbled over a cable, and for a moment she was back in that hotel corridor, the air thick with the sound of metal hitting the floor. She could not catch her breath. Her heart pounded. She was certain that something terrible was about to happen again, even though she knew, rationally, that she was safe. When the attack subsided, she sat on her couch and wept. She was afraid that she would never feel normal again, that the rest of her life would be spent in this state of coiled dread. But beneath that fear was something quieter: the hope that maybe, if she could understand why she had frozen, she could begin to forgive herself.
